title: Reverse proxy, forward proxy, API gateway and CDN
scopeHtml: Scope: forward vs reverse proxy, API gateway responsibilities, CDN basics, cache keys and headers, invalidation, origin shield and the layered request path.

notes.title: Proxies in one picture
notes.html:
A proxy is a middleman that passes requests along on behalf of someone else. Which side it represents gives its name.

  • Forward proxy: represents the client. The client knows about it and sends traffic through it to the internet. Uses: corporate filtering, hiding client IPs, caching, egress control, scraping through rotating IPs.
  • Reverse proxy: represents the server. Clients think they talk to the real site; the proxy forwards to hidden backends. Uses: TLS termination, load balancing, caching, compression, security.
  • API gateway: a reverse proxy plus API-specific jobs (auth, rate limits, routing to microservices, request transformation).
  • CDN: a worldwide fleet of reverse proxies with caches placed near users.

Worked example. A company of 5,000 staff: all web traffic goes via a Squid forward proxy that blocks malware sites and logs access; the public site sits behind an NGINX reverse proxy that terminates TLS and spreads requests over 6 app servers.

Industry examples. Squid, Zscaler (forward); NGINX, HAProxy, Envoy, Apache (reverse); Kong, Apigee, AWS API Gateway (gateway); Cloudflare, CloudFront, Akamai, Fastly (CDN). Service meshes (Istio) place an Envoy sidecar proxy beside every service.

Everyday analogy. A forward proxy is your personal assistant who makes calls on your behalf; a reverse proxy is a company receptionist who takes calls for the staff behind her.

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing up forward and reverse. Ask: who is being hidden, client or server?
  • Calling a load balancer and a reverse proxy different things; an L7 LB is a reverse proxy with balancing.
  • Forgetting each proxy hop adds latency, a failure point and loses the original client IP unless forwarded.

notes.title: Reverse proxy in detail
notes.html:
A reverse proxy sits in front of your servers and handles the jobs that every server would otherwise repeat.

Jobs:

  • TLS termination (one place for certificates).
  • Load balancing and health checks.
  • Connection buffering: it reads the slow client's request fully before opening a backend connection, and sends the response to a slow client while freeing the backend thread. This protects app servers from slow clients ("slowloris").
  • Compression (gzip/brotli), static file serving, HTTP/2 and h3 to clients while speaking h1.1 to backends.
  • Caching of responses, rate limiting, header rewriting, request IDs, WAF.
  • Preserving client identity: adds X-Forwarded-For, X-Forwarded-Proto, or PROXY protocol; the app must trust these headers only from the proxy (otherwise clients can spoof IPs).
# nginx reverse proxy essentials
# location /api/ {
#   proxy_pass http://api_pool;
#   proxy_set_header Host $host;
#   proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
#   proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
#   proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
#   proxy_http_version 1.1;           # needed for upstream keepalive
#   proxy_set_header Connection "";
#   proxy_connect_timeout 1s;
#   proxy_read_timeout 10s;
#   proxy_next_upstream error timeout http_502;   # careful: retries non-idempotent calls
#   client_max_body_size 10m;
# }

Worked example. App server (Tomcat, 200 threads) serves a 2 MB response to a phone on a slow 3G link taking 8 s. Without a proxy the thread is busy for 8 s; 200 such clients block the whole server. With NGINX buffering the response, the thread is freed in ~20 ms and NGINX (event-driven, 10k+ connections per core) handles the slow client.

Industry examples. NGINX fronting Node/Python/Java apps is the default pattern. Envoy powers Lyft, Airbnb and Istio. Cloudflare's own proxy is custom (Pingora in Rust replaced NGINX for them).

Decision gravity. Adding a reverse proxy is cheap and reversible. The risk is trusting X-Forwarded-For wrongly, or auto-retrying POSTs on timeouts (proxy_next_upstream default retries non-idempotent requests only in limited cases; check docs) and causing double charges.

Everyday analogy. The front office of a hospital that takes paperwork from slow walk-ins so the doctors only see ready patients.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing the app sees the real client IP by default. It sees the proxy's.
  • Retrying non-idempotent requests through the proxy.
  • No timeouts between proxy and backend (hung backend ties up proxy connections).

notes.title: Forward proxy and egress control
notes.html:
A forward proxy controls what clients inside a network can reach outside. Clients are configured (or transparently routed) to send traffic through it.

Uses for a designer:

  • Egress allow-list: servers can only call approved domains (stops malware and data exfiltration, and SSRF abuse).
  • Fixed outgoing IPs: third parties allow-list your proxy IPs (payment gateways, partner APIs).
  • Caching of package downloads (Artifactory, Nexus for Maven/npm: faster builds and a supply-chain checkpoint).
  • Audit and DLP, TLS inspection (proxy re-signs HTTPS with a corporate CA; clients must trust it).
  • Anonymity/rotation (residential proxies for scraping, a grey area).
  • HTTPS handling: for HTTPS the client sends CONNECT host:443, and the proxy blindly tunnels bytes unless it inspects.

Worked example. Payments partner only accepts calls from 2 allow-listed IPs. Autoscaling app servers have changing IPs, so route their outbound partner calls through a pair of NAT gateways or Squid proxies with Elastic IPs. Limit: a single NAT IP has about 55k simultaneous connections to one destination IP:port (ephemeral port range), so for heavy traffic use several IPs.

Industry examples. Squid, Envoy as egress gateway (Istio ServiceEntry + egress gateway), AWS NAT Gateway / Network Firewall, Zscaler, corporate PAC files. Many fintechs mandate egress proxies for compliance.

Decision gravity. An egress proxy becomes a critical dependency: if it dies, all outbound calls die, so run it in HA. TLS inspection is a heavy trust decision that also breaks certificate pinning in apps.

Everyday analogy. A company mailroom that checks all outgoing parcels and sends them out under the company's return address.

Common interview traps.

  • Ignoring SSRF: apps that fetch user-supplied URLs should go through an egress proxy blocking internal ranges and cloud metadata IP 169.254.169.254.
  • Making the proxy a single point of failure.
  • Forgetting port exhaustion on NAT / proxy IPs.

notes.title: API gateway
notes.html:
An API gateway is the single entry point for client calls to many backend services, handling the cross-cutting jobs once.

Typical features:

  • Routing by path/host/version to services.
  • Authentication and authorisation: validate JWT/OAuth tokens, API keys, mTLS; pass the verified identity downstream.
  • Rate limiting and quotas per key/user/plan (token bucket in Redis).
  • Request/response transformation, aggregation (one call fans out to several services), protocol translation (REST to gRPC).
  • Observability: access logs, metrics, tracing headers, request IDs.
  • Resilience: timeouts, retries (idempotent only), circuit breaking.
  • Developer portal, versioning, API keys, usage billing.

What it should NOT be: a place for business logic. A gateway full of orchestration becomes a distributed monolith bottleneck owned by one team.

Worked example. 30,000 requests/s with JWT validation. JWT signature verification (RS256) costs about 0.05 to 0.1 ms CPU, so 30k/s = 1.5 to 3 cores. Fine. A per-user limit of 100 requests/min implemented as a Redis INCR with expiry costs one Redis op per request; 30k ops/s is trivial for Redis (100k+ ops/s per node). Gateway adds roughly 1 to 5 ms.

Backend for Frontend (BFF). Instead of one gateway for everyone, a separate thin gateway per client type (mobile, web) shapes responses to what that UI needs. Netflix and SoundCloud popularised this.

Industry examples. Kong, Apigee, AWS API Gateway, Zuul (Netflix, now Spring Cloud Gateway), Envoy-based gateways (Ambassador/Emissary, Istio ingress), Tyk. Uber, Netflix and Amazon all run gateways in front of hundreds of services.

Decision gravity. Choosing a gateway product is a medium-weight commitment (plugins, config format, auth integration). Putting business logic in it is a hard-to-undo mistake. Start with a managed or simple reverse proxy and grow.

Everyday analogy. The security desk and reception of an office tower: check ID, give a visitor pass, direct you to the right floor, and keep a log of everyone who entered.

Common interview traps.

  • Using the gateway as a business orchestrator or a place for heavy transformations.
  • Making auth only at the gateway; services still need to authorise (zero trust, internal calls bypass).
  • A single gateway cluster as a single point of failure or throughput bottleneck.

notes.title: CDN basics
notes.html:
A CDN (content delivery network) caches copies of your content on servers near users, so most requests never reach your origin. Layers: edge (POP) close to the user, optionally a regional/mid-tier cache, then your origin.

Flow: user to nearest edge (anycast or DNS steering); cache hit returns in a few ms; miss goes to the next tier or origin, stores the response (honouring Cache-Control) and returns it.

Good for: static assets (images, JS, CSS, video segments), cacheable API responses, software downloads. Also provides TLS termination close to users, DDoS absorption, WAF, image resizing, and edge compute (Workers, Lambda@Edge).

Key metrics: cache hit ratio (target 90%+ for static, byte hit ratio for large files), origin offload, TTFB, origin egress cost.

Worked example. 100 TB/month of images. CDN hit ratio 95% means the origin serves only 5 TB. CDN egress at roughly $0.02 to $0.085 per GB (varies by volume and provider; confirm current pricing) is often cheaper than origin cloud egress at about $0.09/GB, plus latency drops from 200 ms to 20 ms for faraway users. Raising hit ratio from 90% to 95% halves origin traffic, a huge win at scale.

Industry examples. Netflix Open Connect places its own cache appliances inside ISPs and serves most video from there. Cloudflare, Akamai, Fastly, CloudFront. YouTube/Google Global Cache. Instagram and Facebook photos are served from CDN edges with long-lived immutable URLs.

Decision gravity. Adopting a CDN is cheap and reversible (DNS change). Designing URLs for cacheability (versioned file names) and cache headers is hard to retrofit later; do it early.

Everyday analogy. Instead of everyone driving to the central warehouse, stock popular items in neighbourhood shops and restock them from the warehouse when they run out.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "put a CDN in front" with no cache key, TTL or hit ratio.
  • Caching personalised responses by mistake (leaking one user's data to another).
  • Forgetting that dynamic APIs can also benefit via TLS/connection termination at the edge even when uncacheable.

notes.title: Cache keys, headers and what gets cached
notes.html:
The cache key is what the CDN uses to decide "is this the same request?" Default: scheme + host + path + query string. Anything that changes the response but is not in the key causes wrong content; anything in the key that does not change the response fragments the cache and lowers the hit ratio.

Controls:

  • Cache-Control: max-age=N (browser and shared caches), s-maxage=N (shared/CDN only), public/private (private = browser only, never CDN), no-store (never keep), no-cache (store but revalidate), immutable.
  • Validation: ETag/If-None-Match, Last-Modified/If-Modified-Since give cheap 304 Not Modified replies.
  • Vary: Vary: Accept-Encoding stores separate copies per encoding; Vary: Cookie or Vary: User-Agent explodes the cache. Instead normalise (CDN rules mapping User-Agent to mobile/desktop).
  • Query strings: ignore tracking params (utm_*) in the key, sort them, or whitelist only the ones that matter.
  • Stale handling: stale-while-revalidate=60 serves stale content while refreshing in the background; stale-if-error=86400 serves stale if the origin is down.
Asset:  /static/app.3f9a1c.js     Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable
API:    /v1/products?id=7         Cache-Control: public, s-maxage=30, stale-while-revalidate=60
User:   /v1/me                    Cache-Control: private, no-store

Worked example. Product API /v1/products?id=7&utm_source=ad1 vs ...&utm_source=ad2: with full query strings in the key, 1,000 ad variants of 10,000 products can create 10 million cache entries with near-zero hits. Remove utm_* from the key: 10,000 entries and about 98% hits. Origin load falls from 20k to 400 requests/s.

Industry examples. Cloudflare "cache keys" and "cache rules", CloudFront cache policies (choose headers/cookies/query strings in key), Fastly VCL and Surrogate-Key. Shopify and Stripe docs use immutable hashed assets; news sites use stale-while-revalidate for homepage.

Decision gravity. Cache key design is a one-way-ish door for correctness: a mistake can leak private data, which is a security incident, not a performance bug. Adding a header to the key later is easy; removing a missing one after leaking is not.

Everyday analogy. A library catalogue number: two books with the same number are treated as the same book, so if you leave out the edition number, you hand out the wrong edition.

Common interview traps.

  • Vary: Cookie or caching Set-Cookie responses.
  • Using no-cache thinking it means "do not cache" (it means "revalidate"; no-store is the real prohibition).
  • Letting random query parameters fragment the cache.

notes.title: Invalidation and versioning
notes.html:
"There are only two hard things in computer science: cache invalidation and naming things." Ways to change content that is already cached:

  1. Versioned (fingerprinted) URLs: app.3f9a1c.js or /v42/logo.png. The file name changes when content changes, so you cache forever (max-age=31536000, immutable) and never invalidate. Best option for assets. The HTML that references them is cached briefly.
  2. Short TTL: accept staleness of N seconds. Simple. For APIs: s-maxage=10 with stale-while-revalidate.
  3. Purge by URL or by tag: call the CDN API to delete objects. Fast tools: Fastly instant purge (about 150 ms globally), Cloudflare purge by URL/tag/prefix (seconds). CloudFront invalidations take minutes and the first 1,000 paths per month are free, then paid (confirm current pricing). Use surrogate keys / cache tags (Surrogate-Key: product-7 category-3) so one purge call removes all pages that included product 7.
  4. Soft purge / revalidate: mark stale and refetch in background.
  5. Event-driven: a product update emits an event; a worker calls the purge API.

Worked example. Flash-sale price change must reach users in under 5 s. A TTL of 60 s fails the requirement. Use tag purge on product-7 (about 1 to 2 s on Fastly/Cloudflare), or keep price out of the cached page and fetch it from a tiny uncached/short-TTL endpoint. A mass purge of everything (purge-all) empties the cache and sends 100% of traffic to the origin at once: a self-inflicted outage if origin capacity is sized for 5% miss.

Industry examples. Wikipedia purges pages on edit through its multicast purge system. Fastly's surrogate keys are used by The New York Times and Shopify-class sites. Webpack/Vite fingerprinting on every static build.

Decision gravity. Prefer immutable, versioned content: it makes invalidation a non-problem and rollbacks easy. Reliance on purge pipelines creates an operational dependency and race conditions (purge arrives before the origin has the new data, edge refetches stale data from a lagging replica).

Everyday analogy. Reprinting a menu: either print a new menu with a new version number so old copies are obviously out of date, or send runners to every table to take the old menu away.

Common interview traps.

  • Relying on purge-all as a routine tool.
  • Purging before the origin or its read replica has the new data, re-caching stale content.
  • Not versioning static asset URLs.

notes.title: Origin shield and protecting the origin
notes.html:
An origin shield is an extra cache tier between the many edges and your origin, so a miss in any edge asks the shield first and only the shield talks to the origin. Without it, 200 edge locations missing the same object produce 200 origin requests; with it, 1.

Related protections:

  • Request coalescing / collapsed forwarding: when 1,000 users request the same uncached object at the same moment, the cache sends one request to origin and makes the rest wait for the answer. Prevents the cache stampede / thundering herd.
  • stale-while-revalidate and stale-if-error: serve old content while refreshing or during origin failure.
  • Tiered caching: edge, regional, shield (Cloudflare Tiered Cache, CloudFront Origin Shield, Fastly shielding).
  • Origin lockdown: only the CDN IP ranges or a secret header/mTLS may reach the origin, so attackers cannot bypass the CDN and DDoS it directly.
  • Negative caching: cache 404s/errors briefly (for example 10 to 30 s) so a bad URL hammered by bots does not hit the origin each time.
  • Pre-warming popular content before a launch.

Worked example. Viral video segment requested by 50 edges at once, each missing: without shield, 50 origin fetches for a 4 MB segment = 200 MB; with shield, 4 MB. Origin QPS for a catalogue of 10M objects after a global purge: with 100 POPs and a 20% fill in the first minute, no shield could see 100 x more origin requests than with a shield. Shield cost: slightly higher latency on a miss (one more hop) and small extra fee, usually worth it when origin is expensive or slow.

Production incident pattern. After a deploy or purge, origin CPU and DB connections spike, 5xx rises, and CDN shows a hit ratio drop from 95% to 40%. Metric: origin requests/s versus edge requests/s. Fix: shield, coalescing, staged purge by tag, serve stale on error, rate limit origin.

Industry examples. Netflix's Open Connect fills appliances during off-peak hours to avoid peak-time origin load. CloudFront Origin Shield, Fastly Shield POP, Cloudflare Tiered Cache. Twitter/X and news sites use collapsed forwarding for breaking-news pages.

Decision gravity. Enabling a shield is a reversible config with a small cost. Origin lockdown is something you must do from day one; discovering a leaked origin IP after an attack is painful, and changing the origin IP is a major operation.

Everyday analogy. A wholesaler's regional depot: instead of 200 shops each phoning the factory, the depot orders once and supplies all the shops.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting the thundering herd on a popular uncached object.
  • Leaving the origin reachable directly on the internet.
  • Treating hit ratio as one number; separate static vs dynamic and request vs byte ratios.

notes.title: Putting it together: the request path
notes.html:
A typical modern request passes several of these in order. Knowing which layer does what lets you answer "where do I put X?" quickly.

Where jobs live:

Job Best layer
Static assets, images, video CDN
DDoS absorption, bot filtering, WAF CDN / edge
TLS termination for users CDN edge (short handshake)
Spreading traffic over servers Load balancer
Auth, rate limits, API keys, routing to services API gateway
Per-service retries, mTLS, circuit breaking Service mesh sidecar / client library
Business rules, authorisation of data The service itself
Outbound allow-list, fixed IPs Forward proxy / NAT

Worked example (latency budget). User to edge 15 ms, edge to LB 40 ms (cache miss), gateway auth 3 ms, service 25 ms, DB 5 ms: total about 90 ms. Each extra hop is a few ms, so do not stack three proxies that all do the same thing.

Config example (Envoy-style route). Cache static, pass API:

# Pseudo-config: route table idea
routes:
  - match: { prefix: "/static/" }
    cache: { ttl: 31536000, key: [path] }
  - match: { prefix: "/api/" }
    auth: jwt
    rate_limit: { per_user_per_min: 100 }
    route: { cluster: api_pool, timeout: 5s, retries: { on: [connect-failure], max: 1 } }

Industry examples. Cloudflare/Fastly in front of ALB in front of Kong/Envoy in front of services is common; Netflix runs edge (Open Connect for video, AWS for API), Zuul gateway, then hundreds of services.

Everyday analogy. An airport: the outer road signs (CDN) send most people to the right terminal, security (WAF) screens everyone, check-in desks (gateway) verify tickets, and the gates (LB) assign you to a plane.

Common interview traps.

  • Duplicating the same function (auth, retries) at every layer with different timeouts, causing retry multiplication (3 layers x 3 retries = 27 attempts).
  • Putting heavy logic in the edge or gateway.
  • Not stating timeouts per hop (outer timeout must be larger than the sum of inner ones, or inner retries are wasted).

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Forward proxy represents clients (egress control, fixed IPs, caching); reverse proxy represents servers (TLS termination, buffering, balancing, caching); API gateway is a reverse proxy with auth, rate limits and routing; CDN is a global reverse-proxy cache.
  • Reverse proxies protect app servers from slow clients and centralise TLS; pass client IP via X-Forwarded-For and trust it only from the proxy.
  • API gateway: cross-cutting concerns only, no business logic, avoid single point of failure; BFF per client type is a common refinement.
  • CDN success = hit ratio. Design the cache key carefully (host + path + the few query params that matter), use Cache-Control/s-maxage/Vary correctly and never cache private data.
  • Invalidate by fingerprinted URLs first, short TTL plus stale-while-revalidate next, tag/URL purge when needed; avoid purge-all.
  • Origin shield, request coalescing, serve-stale and origin lockdown protect the origin from stampedes and bypass attacks.
  • Layer the front door (CDN, LB, gateway, mesh) with each job in one place and consistent timeouts and retry budgets.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between a forward proxy, a reverse proxy, an API gateway and a CDN?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: These terms get mixed up. The signal is a crisp rule for which side each represents and where each sits.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A forward proxy represents the client: clients send traffic through it to the internet, used for egress control, fixed IPs and caching. A reverse proxy represents the server: clients think they talk to the site, and the proxy fronts hidden backends for TLS termination, balancing and buffering. An API gateway is a reverse proxy plus API jobs like auth, rate limits and routing to services. A CDN is a global fleet of caching reverse proxies near users.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Test: who is hidden? Forward hides clients; reverse hides servers. An L7 load balancer is a reverse proxy that also balances.

Employee -> Forward proxy -> Internet          (client side, egress policy)
Internet -> CDN -> Reverse proxy -> App        (server side)
Mobile -> API gateway -> Orders / Payments     (reverse proxy + auth, limits, routing)

Each hop adds latency, a failure point, and hides the client IP unless forwarded with X-Forwarded-For or PROXY protocol.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Swapping forward and reverse.
  • Saying an LB and a reverse proxy are unrelated.
  • Forgetting each hop costs latency and needs HA.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where does a service mesh sidecar fit? -> A proxy (Envoy) beside each service, handling mTLS, retries and routing.
  2. Is a CDN a reverse proxy? -> Yes, with caches at many POPs.
  3. When is a gateway too much? -> When it holds business logic or becomes a throughput bottleneck.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer defines the names. The senior places each in the request path and states the cost and failure implications.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams lose the real client IP after adding a proxy hop and break rate limits and audit logs until X-Forwarded-For handling is added.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The most common caching bug is believing no-cache means "do not cache". It shows whether you can control browser and CDN behaviour deliberately.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: max-age is how long any cache may reuse the response; s-maxage overrides that for shared caches like a CDN. private means only the browser may store it, never a CDN. no-cache means store it but revalidate before every reuse; no-store is the real "never keep this". For personal data I use private, no-store.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Asset : /static/app.3f9a1c.js   Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable
API   : /v1/products?id=7       Cache-Control: public, s-maxage=30, stale-while-revalidate=60
User  : /v1/me                  Cache-Control: private, no-store

Revalidation uses ETag with If-None-Match or Last-Modified with If-Modified-Since, giving a cheap 304 Not Modified. stale-while-revalidate serves stale content while refreshing in the background; stale-if-error serves stale when the origin fails. Vary: Accept-Encoding stores a copy per encoding; Vary: Cookie effectively disables sharing.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• no-cache assumed to mean no storage.
  • Vary: Cookie or Vary: User-Agent exploding the cache.
  • Missing private on personalised responses.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Browser cache 1 hour but CDN 5 minutes? -> max-age=3600, s-maxage=300.
  2. How do you cache an HTML page but update quickly? -> Short TTL plus stale-while-revalidate, with fingerprinted asset URLs.
  3. What is immutable for? -> Tells the browser not to revalidate on reload.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer lists directives from memory. The senior designs per content class and knows the safety direction (private/no-store) for personalised data.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A /me endpoint cached at the CDN showed users each other's profiles until private, no-store was set.

questions.contextHtml:
An API sits behind an NGINX reverse proxy that appends the real client address to X-Forwarded-For. A rate limiter (100 requests/min per IP) was added in the app. Attackers bypass it and one scraper made 40,000 requests/min. Code:

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
String clientIp(HttpServletRequest req) {
    String xff = req.getHeader("X-Forwarded-For");
    if (xff != null && !xff.isEmpty()) {
        return xff.split(",")[0].trim();   // first value
    }
    return req.getRemoteAddr();
}
fun clientIp(req: HttpServletRequest): String {
    val xff = req.getHeader("X-Forwarded-For")
    if (!xff.isNullOrEmpty()) {
        return xff.split(",")[0].trim()   // first value
    }
    return req.remoteAddr
}

Nginx config: proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;. Logs show the same attacker with many "client IPs" such as 1.2.3.4, 5.6.7.8.
questions.promptHtml: What is the bug and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use getRemoteAddr()" (that returns the proxy IP, so all users share one bucket), or "block those IPs one by one".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How many proxy hops are in front (CDN, LB, NGINX)? Can clients reach the app directly bypassing the proxy? What does the proxy do with an incoming XFF?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Apply the rate limit at the edge using the proxy's own $remote_addr, which the client cannot forge, and block the scraper at the proxy.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) first XFF value is attacker-supplied, (b) app reachable directly, (c) shared NAT, (d) token-bucket bug.
  4. How I'd verify: curl -H "X-Forwarded-For: 9.9.9.9" https://api/... and check which IP the app logs; examine raw XFF chain spoofed, real-client, cdn-ip.
  5. Root cause: $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for appends to whatever the client sent. The real address is appended by the trusted proxy at the right end; the leftmost value is attacker-controlled. The app trusted the wrong end.
  6. Fix: Count trusted hops from the right: with 2 trusted proxies, the client IP is the entry before them. Prefer the proxy to set a single clean header (proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr and overwrite XFF with $remote_addr at the first trusted hop). Use the framework's trusted-proxy support and accept these headers only from known proxy addresses.
  7. Prevention: Network rule that only the proxy can reach the app; unit tests with spoofed headers; limit by authenticated user or API key as well as IP.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: IP limiting alone punishes users behind NAT; combine with keys. I would not trust any client-supplied header.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Behind a CDN, which IP do I use? -> The CDN's connecting IP header (for example one it overwrites) validated against its published ranges.
  • IPv6? -> Rate limit on a /64 prefix, not a single address.
  • PROXY protocol instead? -> Carries the original address at the connection level, only from trusted senders.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A login limiter was bypassed for months by one header. The fix moved limiting to the edge and trusted-hop counting.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: use remote address.
  • Hire: identifies spoofable leftmost XFF and trusted hop counting.
  • Strong hire: edge limiting, lock down app access, keys plus IP, IPv6 prefixes.

questions.contextHtml: A product API GET /v1/products?id=7 is cached at the CDN with s-maxage=300. Hit ratio is only 31% and origin sees 14,000 requests/s (edge total 20,000 requests/s). Marketing campaigns append utm_source, utm_campaign and a random cb=<timestamp> that a mobile SDK adds. There are 10,000 products. Origin egress cost is a worry.
questions.promptHtml: Why is hit ratio low, what do you expect after the fix, and what could go wrong?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the TTL" (does not fix fragmentation) or "buy a bigger origin".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which params change the response? Is the cache key default (full URL)? Is cb meaningful to the origin? Any personalisation?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident, but origin is under avoidable load; a cache-key change is fast.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) query-string fragmentation, (b) Vary header exploding, (c) responses marked uncacheable, (d) low TTL.
  4. How I'd verify: CDN log: count distinct cache keys per path (millions of variants of 10,000 products); check response headers for Vary and Set-Cookie.
  5. Root cause: With the full query string in the key, id=7&utm_source=a1&cb=123 and ...cb=124 are different objects, each a miss. 10,000 products x campaign variants x timestamps creates endless unique keys.
  6. Fix: Cache key = path + the whitelisted id param only (ignore utm_* and cb, sort the rest). Expected: about 10,000 keys, hit ratio about 98%, origin load falls from 14,000 to about 400 requests/s (2% of 20,000).
  7. Prevention: Dashboard of hit ratio by path; allow-list approach for query params; review of new SDK params.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: If cb is used for debugging cache busting it stops working; keep a documented purge or header. Never remove a param that changes the response (such as lang), or users get wrong content.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Vary: User-Agent present? -> Normalise to mobile/desktop at the edge instead of caching per UA string.
  • Byte hit ratio vs request hit ratio? -> Track both; large objects dominate egress cost.
  • 2% misses still spike at TTL expiry? -> Use stale-while-revalidate and request coalescing.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A hit ratio of 30% looked like a "traffic problem". Whitelisting two query params cut origin cost by about 70%.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: raises TTL.
  • Hire: normalises the cache key and estimates the effect.
  • Strong hire: whitelist approach, Vary handling, byte vs request ratio and risk of dropping meaningful params.

questions.contextHtml: After enabling a CDN, support gets tickets: "I see another user's order history". 11 confirmed cases within 40 minutes. The /v1/orders endpoint returns Cache-Control: public, max-age=60 (added by a framework default for GET) and authentication is by cookie. The CDN default cache key is host + path + query; cookies are not in the key. Origin CPU dropped 60%, which the team had celebrated.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Purge and move on" without treating it as a data exposure event, or blaming users.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which endpoints are affected? How long were they cached? Which responses carry personal data? Which CDN rules and defaults were enabled?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable caching for authenticated paths at the CDN (bypass) now, then purge the affected paths. Treat it as a security incident: engage security and privacy leads.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) public header allows shared cache and the key ignores the cookie, (b) CDN caching despite Set-Cookie, (c) a rule matching /v1/*, (d) another proxy cache.
  4. How I'd verify: curl -I with two different cookies and compare Age and X-Cache: HIT; CDN logs of hits on the path with distinct user cookies.
  5. Root cause: Personalised response marked public plus a cache key that does not identify the user: the first user's response is served to everyone for 60 s.
  6. Fix: Origin sends Cache-Control: private, no-store on authenticated endpoints; CDN configured not to cache requests with auth cookies or Authorization headers; cache only an explicit allow-list of public paths.
  7. Prevention: Default deny at the CDN (cache only listed paths); automated test that a request with a session cookie is never a HIT; security review for CDN rollouts; scope the breach assessment and notify affected users per policy.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Allow-list caching costs some hit ratio but a leak is a security incident. I would not add Vary: Cookie as the fix (it destroys hit ratio and is still risky).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Could you cache the shared part? -> Yes, split the page into a cacheable shell and a private API call.
  • Does private stop a corporate proxy cache? -> Intended to; no-store is stronger.
  • How do you size the exposure? -> CDN logs of HIT responses on affected paths by distinct cookie.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A framework default turned every GET into a public cacheable response. The team adopted default-deny caching and a CI check that fails on public headers for authenticated routes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: purges and moves on.
  • Hire: bypasses, purges, fixes headers.
  • Strong hire: treats it as a security incident, allow-list design, verification tests and exposure assessment.

questions.contextHtml:
A payments partner only accepts calls from two allow-listed IPs. Your autoscaling services route outbound calls through two NAT proxies with Elastic IPs. During a sale the partner call volume rises to 3,000 requests/s, each connection held about 30 s because the partner is slow. Errors start:

connect timeout to partner:443  (rate 18%)
nat: ErrorPortAllocation count rising

Proxy CPU is 10%. The partner confirms nothing is wrong on their side.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Scales proxy CPU or blames the partner.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are connections reused (keepalive) or one per request? How many proxy IPs? Is the 30 s latency the partner's?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Reduce partner-call concurrency with a queue and bulkhead; enable connection reuse; if the partner can allow-list more IPs, add them.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) NAT port exhaustion to a single destination IP:port, (b) partner rate limiting, (c) proxy limits, (d) DNS.
  4. How I'd verify: NAT gateway ErrorPortAllocation and ActiveConnectionCount metrics; ss -s on the proxy; count connections to the partner IP.
  5. Root cause: A NAT IP has about 55,000 usable ephemeral ports per destination IP:port. At 3,000 requests/s with 30 s held connections you need 90,000 concurrent connections; with two IPs you have about 110,000 but traffic is uneven, so one IP saturates and ports linger in TIME_WAIT.
  6. Fix: Short term: keep-alive and connection pooling (HTTP/2 multiplexing if supported), spread across both IPs. Long term: add more allow-listed IPs, set a timeout lower than 30 s, circuit breaker, and ask the partner for a faster SLA or an async API.
  7. Prevention: Alert at 60% of port allocation; capacity model: concurrent connections = rate x hold time.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not just retry (adds connections). More IPs means a new partner allow-list change cycle, so plan lead time.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• SSRF angle? -> The proxy should also block internal ranges and 169.254.169.254 for user-supplied URLs.
  • Single proxy as SPOF? -> Run HA pairs across AZs.
  • TLS inspection? -> Heavy trust decision and breaks client pinning.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A slow partner API turned a modest rate into a port exhaustion incident. Switching to pooled HTTP/2 connections cut ports used by 20x.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds proxy CPU.
  • Hire: connection math and port exhaustion.
  • Strong hire: pooling, extra IPs, backpressure, alerting and HA and SSRF awareness.

questions.promptHtml: How do you update content that is already cached on a CDN? Compare your options.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Invalidation is the hard part of caching. They want a ranked strategy, not "just purge".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: My first choice is fingerprinted URLs like app.3f9a1c.js cached forever, so nothing needs invalidation; only the small HTML that references them has a short TTL. For APIs I use a short TTL with stale-while-revalidate. When freshness matters I purge by tag or surrogate key triggered by an event. Purge-all is a last resort because it sends all traffic to the origin at once.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
1 versioned URL  -> never invalidate, instant rollback by changing the reference
2 short TTL      -> bounded staleness (s-maxage=10 + stale-while-revalidate)
3 purge by URL/tag -> Fastly about 150 ms, Cloudflare seconds, CloudFront minutes (verify)
4 soft purge     -> mark stale, refetch in background
5 event-driven   -> product update -> queue -> purge worker -> CDN API

Surrogate keys let one call purge every page that included product-7. A race to watch: the purge arrives before the origin or its read replica has the new data, so the edge refetches and re-caches the stale version.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Unversioned static asset names.
  • Routine purge-all.
  • Purging before the write is visible on the read path.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do rollbacks work with versioned URLs? -> Point the HTML back to the old hashed file.
  2. Why is purge-all dangerous? -> Hit ratio drops to zero, origin gets 100% of traffic sized for 5%.
  3. How to fix the purge-before-replica race? -> Purge after commit from the replica-visible point, or read from primary for the refill, or short TTL as backup.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "call the purge API". The senior prefers immutable URLs, knows the race conditions and the origin load consequences.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team that routinely ran purge-all at deploy time caused weekly origin brownouts until moving to hashed assets.

questions.promptHtml: What is a cache stampede at a CDN and how do origin shield, request coalescing and stale serving protect the origin?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Strong candidates understand how a cache can amplify load on a miss and what layers prevent it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: When a popular object expires or is purged, thousands of users miss at once and each miss goes to the origin: a stampede. Request coalescing makes the cache send one origin request and hold the others until it answers. An origin shield adds a mid-tier so that 200 edge POPs asking for the same object become one origin request. Stale-while-revalidate and stale-if-error serve old content during refresh or origin failure, and origin lockdown stops attackers bypassing the CDN.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Without shield: Edge x200 -> Origin (200 fetches for one object)
With shield:    Edge x200 -> Shield -> Origin (1 fetch)
With coalescing at each tier: 1,000 concurrent requests per POP -> 1

Worked example: a 4 MB video segment missing in 50 edges is 200 MB from the origin without a shield, 4 MB with one. Costs: one more hop on a miss and a small fee. Other protections: negative caching of 404s for 10 to 30 s, pre-warming popular content, rate limiting origin, and restricting the origin to CDN IP ranges or a secret header or mTLS.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking hit ratio is a single number; split static vs dynamic and byte vs request.
  • Leaving the origin reachable on the internet.
  • No serve-stale policy.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Coalescing downside? -> Waiting requests share the latency of the slow fetch; set a timeout.
  2. How would you detect origin bypass? -> Origin logs with requests not from CDN ranges.
  3. Why negative caching? -> Bots hammering missing URLs otherwise hit the origin every time.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "CDN reduces origin load". The senior explains the failure mode on misses and the layered defences with numbers.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A deploy-time purge dropped hit ratio from 95% to 40% and took the database down; shield plus coalescing plus tag purges prevented a repeat.

questions.contextHtml: You have 40 microservices behind a gateway at 30,000 requests/s. A principal engineer proposes adding order aggregation and discount rules to the gateway "so mobile makes one call". The mobile team agrees; backend teams worry. The gateway currently does JWT checks (RS256, about 0.1 ms each), per-user rate limits in Redis and routing. It is owned by a 4-person platform team. Deadline: 6 weeks.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Sure, put it in the gateway, fewer calls." Ignores ownership, deploy coupling and scale limits.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does the mobile screen need (3 calls or 10)? Who owns the discount rules? What latency budget exists? How often do rules change?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; assess cost. Current gateway CPU for JWT: 30,000 x 0.1 ms = 3 cores; limiter 30,000 Redis ops/s is fine for a Redis node (100k+ ops/s).
  3. Hypotheses (options) ranked: (a) put logic in the gateway, (b) a BFF (backend for frontend) service for mobile that aggregates, owned by the mobile or product team, (c) fix with a GraphQL or composite endpoint in an existing service.
  4. How I'd verify: measure the extra calls and their latency; prototype the BFF; check the gateway deploy frequency vs rule change frequency.
  5. Root cause (of the risk): Business logic in the gateway couples all teams' releases to one platform team and turns a thin front door into a distributed monolith and bottleneck.
  6. Fix (recommendation): Keep the gateway thin (auth, limits, routing, observability, timeouts); build a mobile BFF for aggregation, with discounts remaining in the pricing service. The gateway routes to the BFF.
  7. Prevention: Written gateway scope (what it must never do); contract tests; per-route SLOs.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A BFF is one more hop (a few ms) and one more service to run, but changes ship independently. I would not do auth only at the gateway; services must still authorise (zero trust).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Gateway SPOF? -> Multiple instances across AZs; keep it stateless.
  • Do we need a product gateway or just NGINX? -> Start simple or managed; a gateway product is a medium-weight commitment.
  • Latency added? -> Gateway about 1 to 5 ms; BFF aggregation parallelises downstream calls.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A gateway accumulated discount logic and became the team nobody could release without; extracting it to a BFF took two quarters.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: agrees to put logic in the gateway.
  • Hire: proposes a BFF and keeps the gateway thin.
  • Strong hire: capacity math, ownership and coupling argument, zero-trust authorisation, scope charter.

questions.contextHtml: Flash sale: prices must update for all users within 5 seconds of an admin change. Product pages are cached at the CDN with s-maxage=60. Traffic is 25,000 requests/s with a 95% hit ratio on product pages. The admin writes to a primary Postgres; pages are rendered from a read replica with lag usually 200 ms, up to 3 s under write load. A tag purge API call takes about 1 to 2 s globally.
questions.promptHtml: Design the update path and call out the failure modes.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Lower the TTL to 5 seconds" (origin load rises 12x for these pages) or "purge on write" without thinking about replica lag.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Must every user see it in 5 s or is 5 s a target (SLO)? Is the price shown only on the page or also in cart/checkout? Is price ever allowed to be stale at checkout?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; design. Costs: TTL 5 s would raise origin requests per page from 1 per 60 s to 1 per 5 s per POP.
  3. Hypotheses (options) ranked: (a) tag purge on change, (b) keep price out of the cached page and fetch from a small short-TTL endpoint, (c) short TTL with stale-while-revalidate, (d) purge-all.
  4. How I'd verify: measure end-to-end propagation in staging: write time to edge visibility; replica lag histogram.
  5. Root cause (of the danger): Purge races: purge fires at t=0, edge refetches at t=0.5 s, but the replica is 2 s behind, so the old price is cached again for 60 s.
  6. Fix: Event-driven: price change commits to primary, publishes an event after commit; the purge worker waits until the replica catches up (or reads the refill from the primary using a header) then tag-purges product-7. Better: render the price client-side from a tiny API with s-maxage=3, so the heavy page stays cached. Checkout always reads the authoritative price.
  7. Prevention: Monitor purge-to-visible latency and replica lag; periodic reconciliation job that purges again at +10 s as a safety net.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Purge-all would send 100% traffic (25,000 vs 1,250 requests/s at 95% hit) to the origin. Showing a stale price that cannot be honoured at checkout is a business risk, so checkout re-validates.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Purge API fails or is slow? -> Retry with backoff, and the short TTL on the price endpoint is the backstop.
  • 100 products change at once? -> Batch tag purges; avoid per-URL purge storms.
  • Why not websockets to push prices? -> More infrastructure; polling a cached endpoint is simpler for this need.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A sale price stayed stale for 60 s on a few edges because the purge raced the replica. A delayed second purge fixed it cheaply.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: lowers TTL globally.
  • Hire: tag purge plus awareness of replica lag.
  • Strong hire: decouples price from the page, post-commit events, reconciliation purge, checkout validation, load numbers.

questions.contextHtml:
At 11:02 an engineer ran "purge everything" to fix a bad banner. Metrics:

11:02  CDN hit ratio 95% -> 12%
11:03  origin req/s  1,100 -> 21,000   (origin sized for about 3,000)
11:04  origin CPU 100%, DB connections 480/500, p99 12 s
11:05  5xx 38%, CDN serves errors, retries from clients
11:21  recovery after manual rate limiting and rollback of nothing

No origin shield, no stale-if-error, origin reachable directly.
questions.promptHtml: Lead the review. What failed and what do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Do not run purge-all again." This is a process rule with no guardrails.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Why was purge-all the only tool? What was the bad banner (could be fixed by tag purge)? What is origin capacity at 0% hit ratio? Who can run purges?
  2. Immediate mitigation (what we should have done): Rate limit or queue at the origin, serve stale where possible, ramp traffic back; restore hit ratio via pre-warm of top URLs.
  3. Hypotheses (contributing factors) ranked: (a) purge-all with no guard, (b) origin sized for 5% miss, (c) no shield or coalescing, (d) no stale-if-error, (e) client retries amplified.
  4. How I'd verify: origin vs edge req/s timeline; coalescing metrics; DB pool saturation; the CDN audit log of the purge call.
  5. Root cause: One broad action removed the protection the origin depended on; with 100 POPs misses multiplied (without a shield each POP fetches separately) and no layer absorbed it.
  6. Fix: Tag or URL purge for content changes; soft purge (mark stale, revalidate in the background); enable shield, coalescing, stale-while-revalidate and stale-if-error; negative caching; origin rate limit and a load-shedding mode; lock down the origin to CDN only.
  7. Prevention: Purge-all behind an approval and a staged rollout by region; capacity test at 30% hit ratio; runbook for hit-ratio drop; alert on hit ratio and origin req/s ratio.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Sizing the origin for 0% hit ratio is expensive; better to protect it with shield, staleness and shedding. I would not blame the engineer.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• How to warm the cache after a purge? -> Replay top URLs from logs at a controlled rate.
  • Is stale-if-error always safe? -> Not for prices or inventory; choose per content type.
  • Multi-CDN? -> Different purge semantics; test each.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "just purge everything" button caused two outages in a year. Replacing it with tag purges and a shield made the button unnecessary.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "do not do it again".
  • Hire: finds the amplification and adds shield, coalescing and stale serving.
  • Strong hire: guardrails on the tool, capacity math at low hit ratio, warm-up plan, blameless framing.

questions.contextHtml:
Stack: CDN, ALB, API gateway, orders service, Postgres. A payments dependency slows from 80 ms to 6 s. Settings:

layer        timeout   retries
client app     10 s      3
API gateway     5 s      2
orders svc      3 s      3 (to payments)

Orders traffic is 2,000 requests/s. Within a minute the payments service gets about 50,000 requests/s and falls over; the gateway and orders pods show thread pool exhaustion. A teammate says "payments is just slow, nothing to do".

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blames payments only, or adds more retries "for resilience".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which calls are idempotent? Do retries use backoff and a budget? Which layer owns the deadline? Is there a circuit breaker?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable retries at gateway and client via config or feature flag, shed load, open a circuit to payments and return degraded responses.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) retry multiplication, (b) no circuit breaker, (c) timeouts inconsistent so inner work continues after outer gave up, (d) thread pool sized too small.
  4. How I'd verify: requests-per-incoming at each hop: orders to payments ratio far above 1; tracing shows attempts per request.
  5. Root cause: Attempts multiply: client 3 x gateway 2 x orders 3 = 18 attempts per user action on the payments call path (up to 4 x 3 x 4 = 48 counting the first try at each layer). The 3 s inner timeout with a 6 s slow dependency means every call times out and retries, so load grows as latency grows.
  6. Fix: Retry at one layer only (closest to the failure) with a budget (at most about 20% extra) and jittered exponential backoff; propagate a deadline so inner timeouts are shorter than outer ones and work stops when the outer caller gives up; circuit breaker and bulkhead for payments; idempotency keys so retries are safe.
  7. Prevention: Platform defaults for timeouts and retries; chaos tests that slow a dependency; alert on retry ratio and per-hop request amplification.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Fewer retries means occasional failures surface to users, which is better than collapse. Outer timeout must exceed the sum of inner ones or inner retries are wasted. I would not retry non-idempotent calls without keys.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Hedged requests? -> Can cut tail latency but add load; only with a budget.
  • Load shedding? -> Reject early with 503 and Retry-After when queues grow.
  • Service mesh retries plus app retries? -> A second layer of multiplication; own retries in one place.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A slow dependency multiplied by three layers of retries produced a 25x load spike. One owner for retries and a budget ended the pattern.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the dependency, adds retries.
  • Hire: calculates retry multiplication and proposes a single retry layer with backoff.
  • Strong hire: deadlines propagation, retry budgets, breakers, idempotency, chaos testing and per-hop amplification metrics.
